original_value: The topic of utilizing coupled map lattice to investigate complex spatiotemporal dynamics has attracted a lot of interest. For exploring the spatiotemporal complexity of a predator‐prey system with migration and diffusion, a new three‐chain coupled map lattice model is developed in this research. Based on Turing instability analysis, pattern formation conditions for the predator‐prey system are derived. Via numerical simulation, rich Turing patterns are found with subtle self‐organized structures under diffusion‐driven and migration‐driven mechanisms. With the variation of migration rates, the predator‐prey system exhibits a gradual dynamical transition from diffusion‐driven patterns to migration‐driven patterns. Moreover, new results, the self‐organization of non‐Turing patterns, are also revealed. We find that even in the cases where the nonspatial predator‐prey system reaches collapse, the migration can still drive pattern self‐organization. These non‐Turing patterns suggest many new possible ways for the coexistence of predator and prey in space, under the effects of migration and diffusion.

result.paraphrase: The use of coupled map lattices to study complex spatiotemporal dynamics has drawn considerable interest. To examine the spatiotemporal complexity of a predator-prey system with migration and diffusion, this study proposes a new three-chain coupled map lattice model. Using Turing instability analysis, it derives the conditions under which patterns form in the predator-prey system. Numerical simulations reveal abundant Turing patterns with delicate self-organized structures driven by diffusion and migration. As migration rates vary, the system undergoes a gradual dynamical shift from diffusion-driven patterns to migration-driven ones. In addition, the work uncovers new findings on the self-organization of non-Turing patterns. Even when the corresponding nonspatial predator-prey system collapses, migration can still induce pattern self-organization. These non-Turing patterns point to many new possibilities for predator and prey coexistence in space under the influence of migration and diffusion.
